title: An unusual presentation of Huntington’s disease
case_prompt:
A 59-year-old woman without previous psychiatric or neurological disease presented to the emergency department with pervasive existential anxieties and delusional beliefs of thought insertion and external control, accompanied by audible thoughts. Examination required lorazepam for severe anxiety.  
Laboratory studies revealed mild hypothyroidism (status post–hemithyroidectomy) treated with levothyroxine and hyponatremia from excessive water intake treated with sodium supplementation. Complete blood count, folic acid, vitamin B12, ceruloplasmin, and serologies for HIV, Borrelia burgdorferi, and Treponema pallidum were unremarkable.  
Antipsychotic treatment with risperidone, later switched to chlorprothixene, failed to relieve her delusional ideas.  
Neurological examination showed dysdiadochokinesis (left hand), mild hyperkinetic movements, bradykinesia on finger tapping, and a broad-based gait without rigidity, tremor, or postural instability. She became disoriented to time and place and exhibited long-term memory deficits with episodes of fear, agitation, and perseveration.  
Neuropsychological testing (CERAD+ battery) demonstrated impaired verbal recognition, severe visuospatial dysfunction, reduced semantic and phonemic fluency, and decreased cognitive flexibility; the MMSE score was 22/30 and the FAB score was 10/18. SCID-II showed no personality disorder.  
EEG demonstrated a normal alpha rhythm without epileptiform potentials. Brain MRI revealed generalized cerebral atrophy with putaminal rim sign, a hyperintensity at the lateral margin of the putamen, and ventriculomegaly.  
CSF analysis showed normal tau and beta-amyloid levels, no intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, negative autoimmune encephalitis antibodies, and absence of protein 14-3-3.  
These findings raised suspicion for an underlying neurodegenerative process.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Organic schizophrenia-like disorder was initially diagnosed — “An organic schizophrenia‐like disorder was assumed as the most likely diagnosis…”  
2. Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia was considered because of executive dysfunction and psychopathological symptoms — “clinically predominant executive dysfunction and the described psychopathological symptoms, we considered bv‐FTD as the most likely diagnosis.” It was questioned because “the neurological symptoms displayed by our patient could not sufficiently be explained by bv‐FTD.”  
3. Autoimmune encephalitis was excluded after CSF studies — “the presence of autoimmune encephalitis antibodies … in CSF were excluded.”  
4. Creutzfeldt‐Jakob disease was excluded by CSF marker testing — “protein 14–3–3 in CSF were excluded.”  
5. Progressive supranuclear palsy entered the differential due to striatal hypometabolism patterns — “glucose hypometabolism in the striatum has been observed in atypical Parkinson syndromes, especially in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)…”  
6. Neuroacanthocytosis syndromes were considered for similar PET findings — “glucose hypometabolism in the striatum has been observed in … neuroacanthocytosis syndromes…”
